title: The Aleph-Bet
description: Learn the 22 consonants, their names, final forms, and right-to-left reading.

blocks.caption: Summary
blocks.html:
Biblical Hebrew is written with an alphabet of twenty-two consonant letters, read from right to left. The letters record consonants; the vowel sounds are carried by small marks added much later, written around, above, and below the consonants, and they are not part of the consonant alphabet itself. Five letters — kaf, mem, nun, pe, and tsade — take a different, closing shape when they stand at the end of a word. These are not extra letters but positional variants of the same letter.

Learn the name, the shape, and one consistent transliteration for every letter before moving on. The letter names are themselves old Hebrew words (aleph once meant "ox", bet "house"), and remembering them helps fix the signs in mind. Most letters make a single steady sound, but a few shift: shin can be /š/ or /ś/ depending on where its dot sits, and the six letters b, g, d, k, p, t harden or soften by position in the word — a point studied later as the dagesh.

blocks.caption: Reading right to left
blocks.html: Hebrew lines begin on the right and move left, and a book opens from what an English reader calls the back. Practise the direction on purpose: point at the rightmost letter, name it, then step one letter left. When you meet a whole word, read its letters in that same order. The alphabet itself is recited right to left, beginning with aleph and ending with tav.

blocks.caption: Sound and transliteration
blocks.html: Use one transliteration system and keep it steady. This course writes ʼ for both aleph and ayin, ḥ for het, ṭ for tet, ṣ for tsade, š for shin, and ś for sin. The transliteration is a crutch for the first units only; the aim is to read the Hebrew signs directly. When you write a transliteration, keep the letters in the order you read them.

blocks.caption: Common confusion
blocks.html: Several letters look alike and are easy to confuse: dalet (ד) and resh (ר) differ only by a small corner; bet (ב) and kaf (כ) are similar curves; and he (ה), het (ח), and tav (ת) all carry a top stroke. Distinguish shin (dot on the upper right) from sin (dot on the upper left), and remember that the final forms ך ם ן ף ץ are only the five letters kaf, mem, nun, pe, tsade written at the end of a word.
